title: CONSENSUS IN LANDSCAPE PREFERENCE JUDGEMENTS

findings.antecedent: Mean preference (scenic quality) for landscape scenes
findings.consequent: Variance in preference judgments for landscape scenes
findings.mechanism: Higher preference scenes might lead to quicker, more holistic judgments, resulting in higher consensus.
findings.quote: the means are significantly negatively correlated with the variance (β=-0.83, p<0.001, r² = 0.69).

findings.antecedent: Group differences in respondents' preference judgments
findings.mechanism: Variability is not explained by distinct groups responding differently, but rather by random responding patterns.
findings.quote: the cluster analyses for low and high variance slides in this study did not point to group differences as an explanation for within-landscape variability.

findings.consequent: Proportion of variation in preference judgments
findings.mechanism: Individual differences in perception and evaluation contribute to the overall variability in preference judgments.
findings.quote: the proportion of variation in preference attributable to variation among observers was 26 per cent.

findings.mechanism: A significant portion of variability in preference judgments remains unexplained by scene characteristics or observer differences, suggesting other factors are at play.
findings.quote: unexplained variance (56%) not accounted for by either variation among landscape scenes or variation among observers.

findings.antecedent: Mean pasture likeness (match to mental image of pasture)
findings.consequent: Variance in preference judgments (after accounting for scenic quality)
findings.mechanism: Slides that closely match a strong, commonly shared mental representation of 'pasture' evoke more consistent, quick, and holistic preference judgments, leading to lower variance.
findings.quote: a significant negative correlation between the variance in preference judgements and how well the slide matched the mental image of pasture (β = -0.31, p<0.001).

findings.mechanism: Higher preference scenes tend to have lower variance in judgments, possibly due to more straightforward or holistic evaluation.
Landscapes that closely match a positive, idealized mental image of 'pasture' are generally preferred, reflecting cultural and potentially evolutionary influences.
findings.quote: a significant positive correlation between the means for preference and pasture likeness for the 60 scenes (β=0.53, p<0.001)

findings.antecedent: High pasture likeness (match to mental image)
findings.mechanism: Scenes that strongly match the idealized image of pasture are consistently rated as highly preferred, indicating a shared positive evaluation.
findings.quote: for the slides with the highest pasture likeness the preference means are all high and less spread out

findings.antecedent: Low pasture likeness (match to mental image)
findings.mechanism: Scenes that do not strongly match the idealized image of pasture elicit varied preference judgments, suggesting they are evaluated against other, less consistent mental reference landscapes.
findings.quote: among the slides with the lowest means in pasture likeness there are both high and low preference means.

stimuli.description: 60 color slides of Swedish farmland grasslands (pastures and meadows) taken in summer, sunny weather, clear sky, full daylight

tables.description: Means and variances of preference ratings for 60 landscape scenes, sorted by increasing variance.
Multiple regression results predicting variance of mean preference from mean preference and mean pasture likeness.

limitations: The use of a five-point rating scale might have compressed ratings at the high end, potentially affecting variance for high preference scenes.
The study focused on a single landscape type (pasture), limiting generalizability of findings regarding scenic quality and variance across diverse landscape types.
The study was conducted with Swedish respondents, limiting the generalizability of the 'shared cultural image' hypothesis cross-culturally.
